evidence.text: The second bandstop of Filter 2, between 630-680 nm, attenuates the long wavelength tails of the M and L cone sensitivities, restoring color balance between eyes. A 450 nm longpass filter (Omega Optical, 450LP RapidEdge) was chosen as Filter 1. Filter 2 was optimized using constrained optimization by linear approximation (COBYLA) to minimize the merit function: ΔE/Width bandstop , where ΔE is the color difference between Filter 1 and Filter 2 when transmitting D65 white light and Width bandstop is the spectral width of the short-wavelength band-stop region of Filter 2. This merit function ensures satisfactory D65 color balance between eyes while also maximizing the difference between filters, enhancing their ability to distinguish spectra. For Filter 2, the transmittance of the pass and stop-bands were constrained between 5-15% and 80-95%, respectively, and the longer wavelength stopband was constrained between 600-700 nm to prevent attenuation of the M and L cones at their peak sensitivities (~550 nm, ~580 nm respectively). This procedure yielded an optimized response for Filter 2 with stopbands at 450-500 nm and 630-680 nm, and stopband/passband transmittance of 10% and 90%, respectively; the color difference for illuminant D65 between Filter 1 and Filter 2 is ΔE = 5.21, with chromaticities of (0.348,0.406) and (0.35,0.415), respectively. The required film thicknesses were determined by conventional thin-film optimization methods, including gradual evolution 35 and needle optimization 36 , to implement the target transmission function. The final stack was constrained to be less than 75 total layers, and each layer between 10 and 500 nm thick. The filter was optimized such that the transmission would not change significantly for incident angles up to 5° away from the normal. The films were deposited using ion-assisted sputtering onto an NBK7 glass substrate at a thin-film foundry (Iridian Spectral Technologies, Ontario, Canada). Since the eDCR is caused by the thermally induced photons of a broad spectrum, the use of a narrow bandpass filter should let the signal photons at a specific waveband pass with little attenuation, while blocking the noise photons of all the other wavebands. Because the peak intensity of the blackbody radiation from the fiber at 300K is longer than 2 m, the stopband of an ideal bandpass filter should cover a wavelength range from a few hundred nanometers up to several microns. However, a narrow bandpass filter with a wider stopband is more difficult to design and fabricate than that with a narrower stopband. Considering the wavelength-dependent detection efficiency [16] and a reasonable filter complexity, we designed and fabricated a bandpass filter in the wavelength range of 500-2200 nm with the pass band of 1545-1555 nm. The design principle of the bandpass filter is the interference effect in dielectric multi-layer films [17]. The thicknesses of the Si (SiO2) layers usually range from zero to one wavelength, which corresponds a light wave phase change ranging from 0 to 2π. Using the optical film design software Filmstar tm , the transmittance was calculated based on the transfer-matrix method and the genetic algorithm was performed to optimize the precise thickness of each layer [17][18][19]. The practical bandpass filter is composed of periodic SiO2/Si bilayers alternatively deposited layer-by-layer on the backside of a thermal oxidized Si substrate, which is a popular substrate for the fabrication of SNSPD [9]. The schematic view of the bandpass filter fabricated on the substrate is shown as Fig. 1. The filter is composed of 32 layers, providing a total thickness of 6.02 m. evidence.title: Filters for NIR astronomical photometry: comparison of commercial IRWG filters and designs using OpenFilters
evidence.text: The modern approach of designing filters is based on multi-layer interference filters. A discussion on necessary complexity for realizing IRWG profiles as well the design flow using an open-source filter design software is presented. The basic building block of such filters are alternate stacks of thin films which have alternately low and high refractive indices. The complexity of design and optimization of these filters is best addressed by using specialized software designed for this purpose. To design such filters, the OpenFilters software package was used. OpenFilters is an open-source tool for designing multi-layer thin film filters. This software was developed by the Functional Coating and Surface Engineering Laboratory (FCSEL) and is available as a free design resource from the website https:// www.polymtl.ca/larfis/en/links. The software is open-source. This is beneficial for re-optimizing the designs for different coating/manufacturing technologies and allows for easier collaboration between groups designing these filters. These aspects will be beneficial towards the goal of a common standard of NIR filters. A practical guide to install and use the software is provided by Larouche & Martinu (2008) and useful help in getting started is available in the website. The brief design process for a filter is described as follows: • Initial settings: The initial settings include defining the substrate (typically, fused silica) front and back mediums (typically, void/air) and the wavelength resolution. A wavelength resolution of at least 1 nm is necessary for accurately defining photometric filters. The initial setting is to be done in the Filter: Properties menu. • Filter specification: The process of designing a filter using OpenFilters starts by specifying the exact transmission/reflection curve. Data points of transmission need to be collected from various sources and a smooth filter profile needs to be constructed by spline interpolation. This is an important step as smooth profiles are practically easier to realize by means of multi-layer interference filters. This transmission profile can be given as input to the software from an external .CSV file. The file should contain two columns of data specifying the transmission value as a function of wavelength. A third column specifying the desired tolerance is optional.

evidence.text: Narrowband transmittance filters based on Al/MgF 2 multilayers are another classical coating, which have been used in space instrumentation. They can be designed to peak at any wavelength down to 120 nm. Their main drawback is that peak transmittance is relatively low. Reflective multilayer coatings based on two dielectrics have higher peak performance but lower out-ofband rejection than Al/MgF 2 transmittance filters. The main material combinations are (MgF 2 or AlF 3 )/(LaF 3 or GdF 3 ). Narrowband mirrors based on these materials have been obtained for a wavelength as short as 121 nm (Rodríguez de Marcos et al. 2015) and ~135-140 nm (Zukic and Torr 1992;Gatto et al. 2002). For still shorter wavelengths, a narrowband reflective coating peaked at ~100 nm based on an Al-LiF-SiC-LiF multilayer has been developed (Rodríguez-de Marcos 2013). Its band is suitable to image H Lyman β (102.6 nm) and O VI lines (103.2-103.8 nm) and to reject longer wavelengths like H Lyman α (121.6 nm).

method_findings.reusable_principle: Combine two separate multilayer filters with adjacent suppression bands to achieve broader wavelength suppression than a single filter can provide. Each filter targets a portion of the desired suppression range, and their combined transmittance achieves the full suppression goal.
method_findings.applicability: When single-filter suppression bandwidth is limited (e.g., approximately 100 nm per filter) but broader suppression is required across multiple wavelength ranges such as 355 nm and 1030-1080 nm
method_findings.limitations: Requires fabrication and alignment of multiple filter elements; total system thickness increases; interface losses between filters may affect overall transmittance in passband regions

method_findings.reusable_principle: Replace discrete multilayer interfaces with graded index interlayers that vary composition gradually between high and low index materials. This reduces interface discontinuities and can improve antireflection performance at target wavelengths.
method_findings.applicability: For antireflection applications at specific wavelengths (e.g., 355 nm) on fused silica substrates where conventional multilayer stacks may not achieve desired reflectance targets
method_findings.limitations: Requires precise control of composition gradient during deposition; refractive index profile must be characterized; TMM modeling requires discretization of graded layers into thin sublayers

method_findings.reusable_principle: Start with quarter-wave optical thickness layers (lambda0/(4*n)) for high-reflection bands, then vary optical thickness of selected layers away from quarter-wavelength values through optimization procedures to smooth spectral characteristics and broaden suppression bands.
method_findings.applicability: For cut-off filters and bandpass filters where smoothed spectral characteristics are needed; outer layers can use lambda0/(8*n) thickness for improved performance
method_findings.limitations: Quarter-wave designs inherently have narrow high-transmittance and high-reflection bands; optimization required to broaden bands increases design complexity

method_findings.reusable_principle: Construct bandpass filters using two symmetric dielectric mirror stacks (typically 5 layers each) separated by a resonance cavity layer. Tune center wavelength by adjusting only the cavity thickness while maintaining mirror layer thicknesses constant across multiple filter designs.
method_findings.applicability: For narrow bandpass filters targeting specific wavelengths (FWHM around 10 nm); efficient for designing multiple filters at different wavelengths using same mirror structure
method_findings.limitations: Trade-off between FWHM, peak transmittance, and fabrication complexity; increasing layers beyond 11 may improve performance but increases fabrication difficulty; sideband suppression may require additional commercial filters

method_findings.reusable_principle: Use needle optimization algorithm incorporated into thin-film design software to optimize multi-wavelength high-reflectance coatings with non-quarter-wave optical thicknesses. This enables complex 38+ layer designs targeting multiple wavelengths simultaneously.
method_findings.applicability: For multi-wavelength high-reflectance designs (e.g., 632.8, 810, 1550 nm simultaneously) where conventional quarter-wave stacks are insufficient
method_findings.limitations: Requires specialized optimization software; non-quarter-wave designs are challenging to fabricate with repeatability; layer thickness control critical (quartz-crystal monitor needed)

method_findings.reusable_principle: Select different material pairs for different spectral regions based on absorption and refractive index properties. For UV region near 400 nm, use MgO with high-index material; for visible region, use SiO2 with high-index material. This optimizes filter performance for each target wavelength.
method_findings.applicability: When designing multiple filters across UV, visible, and near-IR regions; material absorption characteristics vary significantly with wavelength
method_findings.limitations: Material optical constants must be characterized or obtained from databases; substrate and incident/exit medium properties influence filter response and must be included in simulations

strategy_plan.planning_summary: This portfolio tests three distinct design strategies for a dual-stopband bandpass filter: (1) UV-centered quarter-wave stacks prioritizing 355-365 nm suppression, (2) visible-centered stacks prioritizing 420-700 nm transmission, and (3) balanced dual-stopband stacks trading between both stopbands. All routes use the same Ta2O5/SiO2 material system and 36-layer maximum, but explore different thickness distribution hypotheses. Literature L01 directly supports the Ta2O5/SiO2 photonic crystal approach; L21 and L28 inform manufacturing considerations for this material pair. The key trade-off is stopband depth versus passband flatness - routes that disagree on which wavelength to center the quarter-wave condition will reveal where the performance boundary lies.

final_answer.problem_interpretation: Design a planar multilayer dielectric filter on a fused silica substrate with unspecified material incidence for an optical detection module. The filter should minimize average transmittance at 355 nm and in the 355-365 nm and 1030-1080 nm bands while maximizing average transmittance in the 420-700 nm band. Constraints include 0 deg incidence, unpolarized light, materials limited to Ta2O5 and SiO2, maximum 36 layers, and individual layer thickness between 20-350 nm. method_findings.reusable_principle: Combine two separate multilayer filters with adjacent suppression bands to achieve broader wavelength suppression than a single filter can provide. Each filter targets a portion of the desired suppression range, and their combined transmittance achieves the full suppression goal.
method_findings.applicability: When single-filter suppression bandwidth is limited (e.g., approximately 100 nm per filter) but broader suppression is required across multiple wavelength ranges such as 355 nm and 1030-1080 nm
method_findings.limitations: Requires fabrication and alignment of multiple filter elements; total system thickness increases; interface losses between filters may affect overall transmittance in passband regions

method_findings.reusable_principle: Replace discrete multilayer interfaces with graded index interlayers that vary composition gradually between high and low index materials. This reduces interface discontinuities and can improve antireflection performance at target wavelengths.
method_findings.applicability: For antireflection applications at specific wavelengths (e.g., 355 nm) on fused silica substrates where conventional multilayer stacks may not achieve desired reflectance targets
method_findings.limitations: Requires precise control of composition gradient during deposition; refractive index profile must be characterized; TMM modeling requires discretization of graded layers into thin sublayers

method_findings.reusable_principle: Start with quarter-wave optical thickness layers (lambda0/(4*n)) for high-reflection bands, then vary optical thickness of selected layers away from quarter-wavelength values through optimization procedures to smooth spectral characteristics and broaden suppression bands.
method_findings.applicability: For cut-off filters and bandpass filters where smoothed spectral characteristics are needed; outer layers can use lambda0/(8*n) thickness for improved performance
method_findings.limitations: Quarter-wave designs inherently have narrow high-transmittance and high-reflection bands; optimization required to broaden bands increases design complexity

method_findings.reusable_principle: Construct bandpass filters using two symmetric dielectric mirror stacks (typically 5 layers each) separated by a resonance cavity layer. Tune center wavelength by adjusting only the cavity thickness while maintaining mirror layer thicknesses constant across multiple filter designs.
method_findings.applicability: For narrow bandpass filters targeting specific wavelengths (FWHM around 10 nm); efficient for designing multiple filters at different wavelengths using same mirror structure
method_findings.limitations: Trade-off between FWHM, peak transmittance, and fabrication complexity; increasing layers beyond 11 may improve performance but increases fabrication difficulty; sideband suppression may require additional commercial filters

method_findings.reusable_principle: Use needle optimization algorithm incorporated into thin-film design software to optimize multi-wavelength high-reflectance coatings with non-quarter-wave optical thicknesses. This enables complex 38+ layer designs targeting multiple wavelengths simultaneously.
method_findings.applicability: For multi-wavelength high-reflectance designs (e.g., 632.8, 810, 1550 nm simultaneously) where conventional quarter-wave stacks are insufficient
method_findings.limitations: Requires specialized optimization software; non-quarter-wave designs are challenging to fabricate with repeatability; layer thickness control critical (quartz-crystal monitor needed)

method_findings.reusable_principle: Select different material pairs for different spectral regions based on absorption and refractive index properties. For UV region near 400 nm, use MgO with high-index material; for visible region, use SiO2 with high-index material. This optimizes filter performance for each target wavelength.
method_findings.applicability: When designing multiple filters across UV, visible, and near-IR regions; material absorption characteristics vary significantly with wavelength
method_findings.limitations: Material optical constants must be characterized or obtained from databases; substrate and incident/exit medium properties influence filter response and must be included in simulations

method_findings.reusable_principle: Construct interference filters using alternating high-low index layer pairs (Bragg reflectors) with a central cavity layer. Typical structure: 5 alternating layers, thick central layer, then 5 alternating layers. Layer thicknesses around 80 nm for visible wavelengths.
method_findings.applicability: For bandpass or color filter applications where moderate bandwidth and good transmittance are needed; compatible with various deposition techniques
method_findings.limitations: Measured spectra may differ from modeled spectra; layer thickness determination requires ellipsometry; performance depends on deposition technique quality

# TMM research and design result

## Problem interpretation

Design a planar multilayer dielectric filter on a fused silica substrate with unspecified material incidence for an optical detection module. The filter should minimize average transmittance at 355 nm and in the 355-365 nm and 1030-1080 nm bands while maximizing average transmittance in the 420-700 nm band. Constraints include 0 deg incidence, unpolarized light, materials limited to Ta2O5 and SiO2, maximum 36 layers, and individual layer thickness between 20-350 nm. Compare different stack designs and analyze trade-offs between passband loss and dual stopband suppression.

## Method research

- **Dual-Filter Suppression Stacking**: Combine two separate multilayer filters with adjacent suppression bands to achieve broader wavelength suppression than a single filter can provide. Each filter targets a portion of the desired suppression range, and their combined transmittance achieves the full suppression goal.
- **Interlayer Graded Index Structure**: Replace discrete multilayer interfaces with graded index interlayers that vary composition gradually between high and low index materials. This reduces interface discontinuities and can improve antireflection performance at target wavelengths.
- **Modified Quarter-Wavelength Optimization**: Start with quarter-wave optical thickness layers (lambda0/(4*n)) for high-reflection bands, then vary optical thickness of selected layers away from quarter-wavelength values through optimization procedures to smooth spectral characteristics and broaden suppression bands.
- **Symmetric Mirror Cavity Tuning**: Construct bandpass filters using two symmetric dielectric mirror stacks (typically 5 layers each) separated by a resonance cavity layer. Tune center wavelength by adjusting only the cavity thickness while maintaining mirror layer thicknesses constant across multiple filter designs.
- **Software-Assisted Needle Technique**: Use needle optimization algorithm incorporated into thin-film design software to optimize multi-wavelength high-reflectance coatings with non-quarter-wave optical thicknesses. This enables complex 38+ layer designs targeting multiple wavelengths simultaneously.
- **Wavelength-Dependent Material Pairing**: Select different material pairs for different spectral regions based on absorption and refractive index properties. For UV region near 400 nm, use MgO with high-index material; for visible region, use SiO2 with high-index material. This optimizes filter performance for each target wavelength.
- **Alternating Layer Bragg Stack with Cavity**: Construct interference filters using alternating high-low index layer pairs (Bragg reflectors) with a central cavity layer. Typical structure: 5 alternating layers, thick central layer, then 5 alternating layers. Layer thicknesses around 80 nm for visible wavelengths.
